claims.text: Geoscientists in Australia are not subject to statutory registration. The Australian Institute of Geoscientists (AIG) runs the voluntary Registered Professional Geoscientist (RPGeo) program - peer-reviewed continuing professional development recognition - and AusIMM offers Chartered Professional accreditation. No Australian jurisdiction mandates a licence to practise as a geoscientist, so professional standing rests on voluntary peer recognition rather than a legal barrier to practice.

sources.title: Registered Professional Geoscientist (RPGeo) Program
sources.whatItMeasured: AIG RPGeo program description - voluntary professional recognition, peer-reviewed CPD.

claims.scope: Voluntary professional recognition (AIG/AusIMM); not a statutory licence. Signals competence to clients/employers, binds nothing legally.
claims.refuteNotes: AIG (peak geoscience body) program page; population = AU geoscientists; voluntary, in force.

claims.text: Jobs and Skills Australia's Generative AI Capacity Study (August 2025) scores 358 ANZSCO occupations on augmentability and automatability using an ILO/Felten-derived task-level framework. It finds that augmentation outweighs automation across the workforce: 79% of Australian workers face low or very low automation risk, while routine clerical and administrative roles carry the highest automation exposure. The study reports professionals and managers (ANZSCO skill levels 1-2) see the highest augmentation potential.

claims.text: A 2026 analysis (aichanging.work, citing the Anthropic Labor Market Report 2026) puts geoscientists - including hydrologists - at 42% AI exposure, 28/100 automation risk, classified 'augment': AI accelerates remote-sensing/satellite, geochemical and geophysical interpretation at scale, but fieldwork, professional judgement and regulatory sign-off keep the role embodied. (US 'licensed professional geologist' sign-off is a US framing; Australian geoscience recognition is voluntary via AIG RPGeo.)
